title: Walking around
hookLine: circling a temple, stupa or mountain clockwise, turning prayer wheels

lines: A STREET THAT ONLY GOES ONE WAY.
cards: Early morning, and the street around the temple is already moving, but nobody is walking straight anywhere. An old man in a sheepskin coat shuffles along, beads clicking through his fingers.
Two teenagers pass him, talking about something on a phone. A woman spins a small handheld drum on a stick as she walks.
Every one of them goes the same way, clockwise, around the same building, and when they reach where they started, some just keep going. It looks like a crowd that lost its map. It's a practice.

teach.b: First, the word. Kora is Tibetan for walking around something holy: a temple, a stupa, a monastery, a lake, a whole mountain.
Tibetan Buddhists walk it clockwise, so the holy place stays on their right, the side of respect. Some walk it every day before work; some circle a whole mountain, a journey of days.
Second, the roots, which are old, and which you met at the stupas in year three.

teach.h: KEEPING THE BUDDHA ON THE RIGHT.
teach.b: In the Pali discourses, visitors who finish speaking with the Buddha sometimes rise, bow, and leave with the Buddha on their right. King Ajatasattu, who came to the Buddha by night, does exactly that before he goes.
Along many kora routes stand prayer wheels, cylinders filled with rolled paper printed with mantras, often om mani padme hum.
Walkers set them spinning clockwise as they pass, or carry small handheld wheels, like the woman in the street.
Tibetan teachers say turning the wheel is like reciting the mantra inside it, and that it carries the wish for all beings to be free of suffering. Fourth, what the circle does.

teach.h: A ROAD THAT GOES NOWHERE NEW.

teach.b: A circle goes nowhere new, and that's the point. Each lap, the same doorways, the same stones, and the mind is asked again and again to come back to the center.
Teachers say a kora can be walked with a mantra, with a prayer, or simply with attention to the feet.

how: Tibetan Buddhists walk kora clockwise around temples, stupas, monasteries and sacred mountains, often reciting mantras, counting beads and turning prayer wheels as they go; some walk a short kora daily and others make long pilgrimages.

o: a slow walking meditation done only inside a monastery
walking clockwise around a holy place, keeping it on your right
a long pilgrimage walked straight to a distant temple

games.q: the circle walk: tap the pairs.
p: the holy place stays on your right
left keeping the Buddha on his right

s: they walk clockwise, so the holy place stays on the right.
prayer wheels are filled with printed mantras
rolled paper printed with mantras, often om mani padme hum.
walking with the holy on your right appears in the Pali discourses
visitors leave the Buddha keeping him on their right, as King Ajatasattu does.

games.q: you've finished one lap around the temple and you're back where you started. you haven't arrived anywhere new. what does a kora walker do?
o: stop, since the walk failed to get anywhere.
turn and walk the other way for balance.
keep going, or finish, without needing to arrive.
games.why: the circle isn't meant to arrive. each lap brings the mind back to the center; some walkers simply keep going.

practice: If you can step outside, walk once around your block, your building or your yard, clockwise, keeping the center on your right; if not, walk slowly around a table or a chair.
Feel each foot land, and keep one thing in mind as your center: a person you love, a wish, or simply the place itself. When you get back to where you started, pause and notice that you're home.

wordCard.voice: Kora. Tibetan for walking around a holy place, clockwise, keeping it on your right, often with beads, a mantra, or a turning prayer wheel. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit pradakshina, walking around keeping something on the right; Tibetans call it kora.

carryVoice: Your line: walk the circle. The circle holds whatever you bring. See you on the next lap.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 2, Samannaphala Sutta, the ending (Ajatasattu bows and leaves keeping the Buddha on his right)
